doc.title: Dave Bailey and John McNeil Interview, 1959-10-25

title: Learning to read music with Chris Kelly and Port Arthur
summary: Bailey took lessons in 1921 with Kelly, read music, played on the steamer Capitol, and went to Port Arthur with the Black Eagle band.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: You know when I started trying to take a lesson? 1921 I was playing Chris Kelly. I was learning good. I was reading the music. I was reading. And everybody in the band could read it. See the trammel player from over the river, he used to buy the music and he arranged it. A brother named Harrison Bowen, he's a wife of Southern Pacific. And that guy was a good musician. Everybody in the band read it. We had Willie Foster. Willie Foster's brother, he was playing, you know, he'd read. And they got there and they showed me my drum pop. He used to hustle right down here, by that cemetery right down on Hallene Street, somewhere down there. And I'd hit that. Made note for note. But they told me I wouldn't need the music no more. So I just stopped. But every once in a while I look at over, I got five pieces of drum music right home now and my dresser drum. And that last drum I played on the steamer cap room. The people all stopped dancing, they all come around me. Where's that drum? The white man and the boss man both said, Son, did you read music right now? I said, no son, I'm just taking the lesson now. He said, well, Bobby Bobby, he said, my drum ain't got nothing on it, but the Zillow for me. You know, the thing made like Terry played them little balls. I told him, I said, allow me to break. I said, I'll play that. He said, I've got to give it to you. He said, you're a drummer. I played places where they can get the people back off me. I said, give me a room to play. And I tell them if they don't get the police to get back, I won't play. I said, I don't like the fair that, the Louisiana fair and the Porn Fair and the Run. He said, wipe over. He said, play a number on the band, on the fair. Play a number on the other people. Crying on the next side of the evening. I actually played the dances and the long part. Couldn't play. I played in Port Arthur, Texas. We played with the Black Eagle band, my brother and I. With E. Van? Yeah, I played with E. Van. So I played, but first we went there with our band.
Well, which was the Black Eagle? I'm trying to get that straight. Is that E. Van Thomas' Black Eagle or was that your ...?

No, E. T. Thomas, they called him that. It was his band. But we went over there, you know. And so we went there, we stayed four months. I think we were headquartered and left here. Put up four months over there, so.
